en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 13.
Mahābyūhasuttaniddesa
Now he will explain the exposition of the Mahāvyūha Sutta:
"Whosoever are addicted to these views,
and declare, 'This alone is the truth';"
All those who are obsessed with views bring upon themselves blame,
yet they also receive praise therein.
Such are these people who are entangled in views.
"Whosoever" (*ye keci*) is a term that encompasses everything in every way, entirely, without remainder,
and exhaustively.
"Entangled in views" (*diṭṭhiparibbasāna*).
There are some recluses and brahmins who are holders of views;
having taken up, mastered, grasped, clung to, and adhered to one or another of the sixty-two types of views, they dwell, live together, abide, and remain according to their respective views—
just as householders dwell in houses, or those with offenses dwell amidst offenses, or those with defilements dwell amidst defilements.
This being so, some... live together— those who are addicted to views.
“They say, ‘This alone is the truth’ means:
they say, speak, utter, illuminate, and express, ‘The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain.
‘The world is non-eternal’ … [and so forth].”
“After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, all else is vain”—thus they say, speak, declare, explain, and communicate, asserting, “This alone is the truth.
All of them bring upon themselves censure.
All those ascetics and brahmins pursue only blame, pursue only censure, and pursue only ill-repute;
all of them become only blamed, only censured, and only ill-reputed— it is because they all bring blame upon themselves.
"And they obtain praise there as well.
Therein, by means of their own view, their own inclination, their own preference, and their own conviction, they obtain, acquire, approach, and find praise, eulogy, fame, and renown;
thus it is said: "And they obtain praise there as well."
Therefore that created being said:
“Whosoever these are who are immersed in views,
and who declare, ‘This alone is the truth’;”
“They all bring censure upon themselves, yet they also receive praise therein. For this is but little;
it is not enough for equanimity.
I declare that there are two fruits of dispute;
seeing this, one should not engage in dispute,
beholding the secure ground of non-dispute.
"For this is trifling; it does not suffice.
"For this is trifling" means: this is small, this is inferior, this is meager, this is base, this is a mere tetrad, this is limited—thus, "for this is trifling."
It is not sufficient for equanimity; it is not sufficient for the equanimity of lust, the equanimity of hatred, the equanimity of delusion,
anger, resentment, contempt, insolence, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance,
intoxication, or negligence— it is not sufficient for all the defilements.

"For the sake of the allaying, the subsiding, the calming, the extinction, the relinquishing, and the tranquilization of all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations"—
this is indeed not little, for it is sufficient for allaying.
"I shall declare the two fruits of dispute.
There are two fruits of a quarrel over views, a strife over views, a conflict over views, a dispute over views, and a contention over views: there is victory and defeat;
there is gain and loss; there is fame and infamy; there is blame and praise; and there is pleasure and pain.
There is joy and grief; there is the desirable and the undesirable; there is attraction and repulsion; there is elation and dejection;
there is compliance and opposition. Or else, that karma leads to rebirth in hell, leads to rebirth in the animal realm, or leads to rebirth in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
"I speak, I declare, I teach, I prescribe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, I elucidate"—
thus do I speak of two fruits of dispute.
Having seen this as well, one should not dispute.

"Having seen this" means: having seen, observed, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest this danger—namely, in quarrels over views, disputes over views, conflicts over views, controversies over views, and wranglings over views—one should not engage in controversy.
One should not create a quarrel, one should not create a dispute, one should not create a conflict.
One should not engage in dispute; one should not create contention. One should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, and contention.

One should be detached from, abstain from, refrain from, have emerged from, escaped from, and be liberated from quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, and contention; one should dwell with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
Having seen this too, one should not dispute.
"Beholding the secure state, the ground of non-dispute":
the ground of non-dispute is said to be the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna— seeing, beholding, looking upon, contemplating,
and examining this as the ground of non-dispute, as security, as protection, as a shelter, as a refuge, as fearlessness, as the deathless, as the immortal, as Nibbāna—
one is "beholding the ground of non-dispute as security."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Truly, this is but little and not enough for peace;
I declare that there are two fruits of dispute:”
"Having seen this too, one should not dispute,
beholding the state of security which is free from dispute.
Whatever these various conventional designations of ordinary people may be—
The wise person does not enter into any of these;
being free from attachment, how could he resort to attachment,
failing to exercise patience toward what is seen and heard?
"Whatever conventions there are among worldlings":
"whatever" (*yā kāci*) is a term that exhaustively includes everything in every way, entirely, without remainder, and without exception— this is what "whatever" signifies.
"Conventional designations" (*sammutiyo*): "conventional designations" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views, which are called "designations of views.

They are called "worldly conventions" (*puthujjā*) because they are conventions produced by worldlings (*puthujjana*); or alternatively, they are called "worldly conventions" because they are conventions produced by various different people (*puthu nānājanehi*).
"Whatever these various conventional designations of ordinary people may be,
the wise one does not enter into any of them. The "wise one" is one who has attained true knowledge, who possesses insight, who is discerning, and who is intelligent.

"One leads away from all these conventional designations of views; one does not approach them, does not go toward them, does not grasp them, does not misapprehend them, and does not adhere to them"—thus, the wise person does not approach any of these.
Being without clinging, how could he cling?
There are two kinds of clinging:
clinging to craving and clinging to views... [as before] ...this is clinging to craving... [as before] ...
This is the approach of views.
For him, the approach of craving has been abandoned and the approach of views has been relinquished.

Because the approach of craving has been abandoned and the approach of views has been relinquished, by being free from approaches, what form would a person approach, go toward, grasp, cling to, or adhere to as "this is my self"?
What is feeling?
… What is perception?
… What are volitional formations? …
What is consciousness?
... What is destiny?
... What is rebirth? ...
What is rebirth-linking?
… What is existence?
… What is saṃsāra?
"What would he take up, approach, grasp, cling to, or adhere to as a cycle?"— being one who does not take up, how could he resort to taking up?
"Not forming a conviction regarding what is seen or heard."
Not forming approval regarding what is seen or purification through what is seen, not forming approval regarding what is heard or purification through what is heard,
not forming approval regarding what is sensed or purification through what is sensed— not producing, not generating, not bringing about, and not causing to arise desire, affection, or lust.
Not finding satisfaction in what is seen or heard.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Whatever these conventional designations of the world may be..."
The wise person does not enter into any of these;
being free from attachment, how could he resort to attachment,
failing to exercise patience toward what is seen and heard?
Those for whom virtue is supreme say that purity comes through restraint;
they remain established, having undertaken their vows.
Let us train right here in this very teaching for the sake of its purification.
"Those who have reached existence, who proclaim virtuous conduct,
say that purity comes through the excellence of morality and restraint.
There are some recluses and brahmins who maintain that the excellence of morality is the highest.

By mere virtue, mere restraint, mere self-control, and mere non-transgression, they claim, say, speak, declare, illuminate, and maintain that there is purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and complete emancipation.
The ascetic Muṇḍikāputta says thus:
“Householder, I describe a person endowed with four qualities as one perfected in skill, supremely skilled, who has attained the highest goal, an unshakable ascetic.”
"By which four?
Here, householder, one does not commit an evil deed with the body, does not utter evil speech, does not entertain evil intentions, and does not live by an evil livelihood.
It is by these four qualities, householder, that I describe a person as a perfected practitioner of the wholesome, supremely wholesome, who has attained the highest goal, an unshakable ascetic."
"This being so, there are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim the supremacy of virtue;

they declare, speak, talk, say, illuminate, and express that purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation are attained through mere virtue, mere self-restraint, mere restraint, and mere non-transgression.
Thus they say that purity comes through self-restraint, holding virtue to be supreme.
"Having undertaken a vow, he stands firm":
"Vow" (vata) means either the vow of an elephant, or the vow of a horse, or the vow of a cow, or the vow of a dog, or the vow of a crow, or the vow of Vāsudeva,
or the vow of Baladeva, or the vow of Puṇṇabhadda, or the vow of Maṇibhadda, or the vow of Agni, or the vow of a Nāga.
or the vow of the Supaṇṇas, or the vow of the Yakkhas, or the vow of the Asuras, or the vow of the Gandhabbas, or the vow of the Great Kings,
or the vow of the Moon, or the vow of the Sun, or the vow of Indra, or the vow of Brahmā, or the vow of the gods, or the vow of the Directions—
having taken it up, having undertaken it, having grasped it, having adopted it, having clung to it, and having adhered to it— it remains present.
"Present, attached, approached, clung to, and intent upon"—
having undertaken the vow, they have established themselves thus:
"Right here we shall train for the sake of its purification."
"Here" means by one's own view, by one's own inclination, by one's own preference, and by one's own tenet.
"We would train" means we would train, we would practice, we would fully practice, and having undertaken it, we would live accordingly— that is,
we would train right here.
"Now, let us train right here for his purification"—that is, for his purity, complete purity, cleansing, liberation, full liberation, and total release;
"let us train right here for his purification.
"Those skilled in the noble life, led by existence... [so it is said].
"Led by existence" means led by existence, gone to existence, obsessed with existence, and intent upon existence— thus they are "led by existence.

"Speakers of what is wholesome" means speakers of the wholesome, speakers of the wise, speakers of the steadfast, speakers of the method, speakers of causes, speakers of characteristics, speakers of reasons, speakers of grounds, and speakers according to their own tenets.
They are brought about by existence and consist of wholesome declarations.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Those for whom virtue is supreme say that purity comes through restraint.”
Having undertaken the training and established themselves therein,
let us train right here for its purification,
being led toward existence and dedicated to what is wholesome.”
If one has passed away from a state of virtue,
one trembles, having failed in one's karma;
one yearns and aspires for purity.
"The Teacher himself, having fallen away, dwells abroad from his home.
If he has fallen away from virtue and the precepts"—
he falls away from virtue and the precepts for two reasons:
One passes away either by being interrupted by another, or by failing to achieve one's goal.
How does one pass away by being interrupted by another?
Another interrupts [one’s confidence]: "This teacher is not omniscient; the Dhamma is not well-expounded; the Saṅgha is not practicing rightly."
The view is not auspicious, the practice is not well-proclaimed, the path does not lead out;
herein there is no purity, no purification, no complete purification, no liberation, no emancipation, no total emancipation;
herein they are not purified, not cleansed, not completely cleansed, they are not liberated, not emancipated, not totally emancipated; it is inferior.
"Inferior, low, base, inferior, and limited"— thus does the other interrupt.

Being thus interrupted, he falls away from the Teacher, falls away from the teaching of the Dhamma, falls away from the Saṅgha, falls away from right view, falls away from the practice, and falls away from the path.
Thus one passes away through the cutting off of others.
How does one pass away by failing to fulfill?
Failing to fulfill virtue, one passes away from virtue; failing to fulfill vows, one passes away from vows; failing to fulfill both virtue and vows, one passes away from virtue and vows.
Failing thus to accomplish it, one passes away; if,
having passed away, one is reborn among those possessed of virtue,
one trembles because of having failed in one's duty.

“He trembles” means: he trembles, quivers, and shakes violently, thinking of his virtue (*sīla*), vow (*vata*), or both virtue and vow (*sīlabbata*): “I have failed, I have missed the mark, I have stumbled, I have slipped; having lost my way, I have failed. Thus, he trembles. “Having failed in karma” means:
having failed in the formative action of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), the formative action of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), or the formative action of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).
Or, thinking, "I have failed, I have erred, I have stumbled, I have slipped; having misunderstood,
I have gone astray," one trembles, quivers, and shakes violently—
thus one "quivers" because of having failed in one's duty.
"He yearns and aspires for purity. "He yearns" (*pajappati*) means:

he utters a vow regarding virtue, or he utters a vow regarding ascetic observance, or he utters a vow regarding both virtue and ascetic observance; he yearns, he yearns intensely, he yearns with longing—thus, "he yearns."

"And he yearns for purity" means: he yearns for purity of virtue, or he yearns for purity of observances, or he yearns for purity of both virtue and observances; he longs for it, desires it, and craves it—thus, "he yearns and yearns for purity.
"Like a teacher who has fallen away while living abroad from his home..."
Just as a man who has departed from his home and is living abroad with a caravan might find that caravan stranded and either follow after it or return to his own home;
even so, that holder of views might take up that teacher or take up another teacher,
take up that teaching or take up another teaching, or take up that group or another group.
Or he takes up that group and clings to it, or takes up another view; or he takes up that practice and clings to it, or takes up another practice;
or he takes up that path and clings to it, or takes up another path—he misapprehends and adheres to it.
One who has fallen away from virtue while living abroad from home is indeed lost.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If one has passed away from those possessed of virtue..."
Having failed in his duty, he is tormented;
he yearns and longs for purity,
like a teacher who has fallen from his home while living abroad.
Having abandoned all rules and observances,
as well as this karma— both blameworthy and blameless—
he does not long for purity or impurity.
"Let one who is dispassionate live for the sake of attaining peace,
having abandoned all rules and observances.
Having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence all purifications of virtue.
Having abandoned, having relinquished, having dispelled, having brought to an end, having made non-existent all purifications through vows;
having abandoned, having relinquished, having dispelled, having brought to an end, having made non-existent all purifications through rules and vows—
thus, "having abandoned all rules and vows."
"And kamma is both blameworthy and blameless.
Blameworthy kamma is said to be dark with dark result.
"Blameless action" is said to be white with white result.
Having abandoned both blameworthy action and blameless action— having relinquished them, dispelled them, brought them to an end, and made them non-existent— [one dwells].
And this action is both blameworthy and blameless.
"One who does not seek purity or impurity":
they seek impurity, they seek unwholesome states.
"Seeking purity" means they seek purity; they seek the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Seeking impurity" means they seek unwholesome states; they seek the five strands of sensual pleasure.

"Seeking purity" means they seek the sixty-two types of views; "seeking impurity" means they seek unwholesome states, they seek the five strands of sensual pleasure, and they seek the sixty-two types of views.
They aspire to purity;

they aspire to wholesome states pertaining to the three realms, yet they aspire to impurity, they aspire to unwholesome states, they aspire to the five strands of sensual pleasure, they aspire to the sixty-two views, and they aspire to wholesome states pertaining to the three realms;
they aspire to purity; and ordinary good persons aspire to the entry into the fixed course of rightness.
Those in training aspire to the supreme state, which is arahantship.

Once arahantship is attained, the arahant no longer aspires to unwholesome states, nor does he aspire to the five strands of sensual pleasure, nor does he aspire to the sixty-two views, nor does he aspire to wholesome states within the three realms. Nor...
He aspires neither to the entry into the path of assurance (*niyāma*) nor to the supreme state of Arhatship.
Having transcended aspiration, the Arhat has passed beyond increase and decrease.
He has completed his residence [in the training], fulfilled his practice... [and so forth].
"There is no cycle of birth, aging, and death; for him there is no further becoming"—
thus, not seeking purity or impurity,
one should live detached, upholding peace.

"Abstinent": one who is far removed from purity and impurity is abstinent (*virata*), refrained, desisted, emerged, escaped, and liberated; he dwells with a mind whose boundaries have been transcended—thus he is "abstinent.
"He conducts himself" (*carati*): he may conduct himself, move about, roam, dwell, behave, persist, endure, or maintain himself—thus [it is said].
"One should live abstaining, upholding peace.
By "peace," sixty-two types of speculative views are meant; one who does not grasp at, does not cling to, and does not adhere to these views of peace—[that is what is meant].
Let one who is detached live for the sake of attaining peace.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having abandoned all rules and observances...”
“Action, both blameworthy and blameless—
without desiring purity or impurity therein,
one should live detached, not grasping at peace.”
Depending on that, those who are heading upstream praise purification—
whether it be something loathsome, or what has been seen, heard, or sensed.
They are not free from craving for various states of existence.
Depending upon that [craving], they are disgusted by asceticism.

There are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim asceticism and self-disgust as their doctrine, who hold asceticism and self-disgust as their essence, who rely upon asceticism and self-disgust; they are unsteady, clinging, attached, drawn near, obsessed, and intent upon them.
"Depending upon that which is loathsome," or alternatively, "seen, heard, or sensed. This means:

depending upon, relying upon, grasping, misapprehending, and adhering to what is seen or the purification of what is seen; what is heard or the purification of what is heard; what is sensed or the purification of what is sensed.
"Or else, regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed:
'Those who look upward proclaim purity'—
there are some recluses and brahmins who hold such views."
Which are those recluses and brahmins who proclaim upward movement?
Those recluses and brahmins who are proponents of ultimate purity, proponents of purity through the cycle of rebirth, holders of the view of non-action, and eternalists—
these are the recluses and brahmins who proclaim upward movement.
In this saṃsāra, they praise, speak, discuss, declare, explain, illuminate, and express purity, complete purity, absolute purity, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation— thus,
"those who go upward praise purity. They are those whose craving for various states of existence has not been removed.
Craving means craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.

"In various states of existence" means in various states of becoming: in a state of becoming as action and in a state of renewed becoming as sensual desire; in a state of becoming as action and in a state of renewed becoming as sensual desire, and in a state of becoming as form;

in a state of becoming as action and in a state of renewed becoming as form, and in a state of becoming as the formless; in a state of becoming as action and in a state of renewed becoming as the formless.
In repeated becoming, in repeated destinies, in repeated births, in repeated rebirths, in the repeated production of individual existence—

one who is not free from craving, not devoid of craving, not cast off craving, not rid of craving, not released from craving, not abandoned craving, not relinquished craving— such a one is "one who has not overcome craving for various states of existence."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Depending on that, whether it be something loathsome,
Or else something seen, heard, or sensed;”
"Those who look upward boast of purity;
they are not free from craving for various states of existence.
For the utterances of one who yearns and longs—
Or even that which is stirred up among those things one has planned;
for him who has neither passing away nor rebirth here,
by what could he be stirred, or where could he lament?
"For one who yearns, there are utterings" means that "yearning" (patthanā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
It is lust, infatuation... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Of one who longs" means: of one who longs, who desires, who approves of, who yearns for, who passionately craves—of such a one who longs.
"Longings" means: [the objects of] those cravings.
“Longing” (jappanā) is a term for craving.
It is that which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness—
the longings of one who is yearning.
"Or even what has been cast away among things fashioned.
"Fashioning" refers to two kinds of fashioning:
the fashioning of craving and the fashioning of views... [and so forth].
This is the fabrication of craving... [and so on] ...this is the fabrication of views.
"Or even wavering among those things fabricated."
They tremble when they fear the confiscation of a planned object; they tremble while it is being confiscated; they tremble when it has been confiscated.

They tremble when they fear the alteration of a planned object; they tremble while it is being altered; they tremble when it has been altered; they quiver, they shake violently—thus, "they tremble even regarding what was planned."
"Cutūpapāto idha yassa natthīti": "For whom there is no passing away and rebirth here.
"For whom" refers to the Arahant whose taints are exhausted.
For whom there is going and coming, going-and-coming, time, destiny, existence and non-existence, death, and rebirth—that is, arising.
And for whom there is no passing away, no rebirth, no birth, and no aging-and-death— these do not exist, they are not present,
they are not found, they are not apprehended; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—
such a one has here no passing away and no rebirth.
By what would he be pierced, or where would he lament?
By what passion would he be pierced? By what hatred would he be pierced? By what delusion would he be pierced?
By what conceit would he be pierced? By what view would he be pierced? By what restlessness would he be pierced? By what doubt would he be pierced?
By which underlying tendencies would one be pierced—
as "lustful," or "hateful," or "deluded," or "bound," or "clinging," or "distracted," or "fallen into the undesirable," or "firmly rooted"?
Those volitional formations have been abandoned.

With the abandoning of volitional formations, by what could one be affected regarding a destination—as a denizen of hell, or an animal, or a ghost, or a human, or a deva; or as one possessing form, or formless;
or as percipient, or non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient? That cause does not exist; that condition does not exist.
"There is no cause, there is nothing by which one would tremble, shudder, or shake violently"—by what, then, would one tremble?
"Where does one wail, or where might one wail; for what might one wail? Where would one wail, lament, or cry out intensely?"—[this is said].
By what could he be pierced, or where could he lament?
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For one who still yearns, there are lamentations...”
Or even that which is stirred up among things contrived;
for him who has neither passing away nor rebirth here,
by what could he be stirred, or where would he lament?
Some call this Dhamma supreme,
while others call that very same thing inferior;
which of these two statements is the truth?
For all these are proponents of what is wholesome.
Regarding that which some call the supreme Dhamma—
whatever Dhamma, view, practice, or path certain recluses and brahmins declare, "This is the supreme, the highest, the best"— [they hold this to be so].
"Exalted, preeminent, supreme, and sublime"— thus they say, thus they speak, thus they declare,
thus they illuminate, thus they express themselves:
"That which some call the Dhamma that is highest."

"But they say that very thing is inferior" means: regarding that very same Dhamma, view, practice, and path, some ascetics and brahmins say, "This is inferior, this is base, this is low, this is wretched, this is fourfold, this is limited";
thus they speak, thus they discourse, thus they declare, thus they elucidate, thus they express themselves.
"But others say that they kill only him.
"Which of these statements is the true one? [he asked.
"Among these ascetics and brahmins, which statement is true, real, factual, as it is, according to reality, and unerring?"—thus he inquired.
"Which among these is the true doctrine?
For all of them indeed proclaim what is wholesome.

[He thought: "All these ascetics and brahmins proclaim what is wholesome, they proclaim the wise, they proclaim the steadfast, they proclaim the methodical, they proclaim the causal, they proclaim the characteristic, they proclaim the reason, they proclaim the foundation, each according to their own tenets."
All these indeed are proclaimers of what is wholesome.
Therefore that created being said:
“Some call this Dhamma supreme;”
"But others say that he alone is base.
Which of these statements is true?
For all of them claim to speak of what is wholesome."
For they say their own doctrine is complete,
while they call the doctrine of another inferior;
thus, having quarreled, they dispute.
"Each one calls their own convention truth.

For some recluses and brahmins say, "Our own doctrine is complete," meaning they say of their own doctrine, view, practice, and path, "This is sufficient, complete, and unsurpassed," and so they speak thus...
[and so on] ...thus do they express themselves.
For they say that their own teaching is complete, but they say the teaching of others is inferior.
Regarding the teaching, view, practice, and path of others, some ascetics and brahmins say: "This is inferior, this is base."
"This is inferior, this is base, this is fourfold, this is limited"— thus they say, thus they speak,
thus they utter, thus they illuminate, thus they express:
"They call the Dhamma of another inferior."
"Thus quarreling and disputing" means: having thus grasped, taken up, seized, clung to, and adhered to [their views], they dispute;
they engage in strife, engage in quarreling, engage in contention, engage in disputation, and engage in conflict, saying:
"You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... [and so on]."
"Or explain it away, if you are able"—
thus they dispute, quarreling;
each proclaims their own respective convention as the truth.
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false”—thus they each declare their own conventional view to be the truth.
“The world is not eternal…” [and so forth].
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’—thus they each assert their own respective conventional truth.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For their own doctrine they say it is complete,
but for the doctrine of another they say it is inferior;
thus, having quarreled, they dispute.”
"Each one declares their own convention to be the truth.
If one were inferior merely because of disparaging another,
no one would ever excel in the Dhammas.
For many indeed speak of another's doctrine as inferior, speaking with great insistence. If,

by means of disparaging another, thinking "he is inferior"— for the sake of disparaging another, for the sake of censuring, for the sake of reviling, for the sake of upbraiding— one thinks that another is a fool, inferior, base, lowly, wretched, contemptible, or insignificant— [then one is at fault].
"If one is base because of reviling another,
no one would be distinguished in terms of qualities"—
that is, no one would be foremost, best, superior, preeminent, supreme, or excellent in terms of qualities.
No one would be distinguished among the teachings.
For many speak of the Dhamma to others as being inferior;
even many people speak of the Dhamma to many, disparaging it, censuring it, reviling it, and denouncing it as inferior, base, and low.
Many speak of the Dhamma to one person, disparaging, censuring, reviling, and condemning it as inferior,
base, lowly, wretched, limited, and trifling; and one also speaks of the Dhamma to many people,
disparaging, censuring, reviling, and condemning it as inferior, base, lowly, wretched, limited, and trifling.
Even one person speaks of the Dhamma to another, speaking disparagingly, censuring, reviling, [saying it is] inferior,
base, low, wretched, fourfold, and limited— for indeed,
they speak of the Dhamma to others in various ways.
"Inferior yet speaking firmly":

one's own faction (*sakāyana*) is the Dhamma, one's own faction is the view, one's own faction is the practice, one's own faction is the path. Those who speak firmly, speak steadfastly, speak powerfully, and speak with persistence regarding their own faction are "inferior yet speaking firmly."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“If one is inferior because of reviling another,
no one would be distinguished in terms of the Dhamma.”
"For they preach the Dhamma to others as something distinct,
speaking with firmness from their own lowly standpoint.
Even their worship of the True Dhamma is just like that.
Just as they praise their own respective doctrines,
so too would all doctrines be true,
for their purity is indeed individual.
Their worship of the True Dhamma is likewise.
What is the worship of the True Dhamma?
One honors, reveres, respects, and worships one’s own Teacher, thinking: "This Teacher is omniscient."

This is worship of the true Dhamma: honoring, respecting, revering, and worshipping one’s own teaching, one’s own group, one’s own view, one’s own practice, and one’s own path, thinking, “This is the path that leads to liberation”—
this is worship of the true Dhamma.
"Even their worship of the True Dhamma is likewise" means that the worship of the True Dhamma is thus— true, real, factual, as it is,
and unerring— thus, "even their worship of the True Dhamma is likewise.
It is just as they praise their own respective [doctrines].

The Dhamma belongs to one’s own faction, the view belongs to one’s own faction, the practice belongs to one’s own faction, the path belongs to one’s own faction; they praise, extol, laud, and commend their own factions—thus is it that they praise their own factions.
"May all doctrines be true" means: may all doctrines be such as they are, real, actual, according to fact, and non-perverted.
All doctrines would be true, for their purity is indeed individual.
For those recluses and brahmins, purity, complete purity, and utter purity; liberation, complete liberation, and utter liberation are each individual.
For their purification is indeed personal.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Even their worship of the True Dhamma is likewise so.”
Just as they praise their own respective views,
so too would all doctrines be true,
for their purity is indeed individual.”
The Brahmin has no need for others to lead him;
he has grasped the definitive conclusions regarding all phenomena.
Therefore, he has transcended all disputes.
"For he does not see any other Dhamma as supreme;
for a brahmin there is nothing to be led by another"—
this is not a negation.
A "brahmin" is so called because he has banished (*bāhitatta*) seven things... [as above] ...he is unattached, such-like;
he is called a brahmin. For a brahmin there is no state of being led by others;

a brahmin is not led by others, he does not follow the authority of others, he is not dependent on others, and he is not bound to others. He knows and sees, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful.

“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’: for a brahmin there is no dependence on others; the brahmin is not led by others, does not follow the authority of others, does not rely on others, and is not bound to others. He knows and sees, undeluded, clearly comprehending and mindful.
‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’ …pe… ‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’: for a brahmin there is no dependence on others.”
A brahmin is not led by others, does not rely on others, does not depend on others, and is not bound to others; he knows and sees, undeluded,
clearly comprehending and mindful— thus, for a brahmin, there is no state of being led by others.
"Having thoroughly determined among phenomena" (*dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītan*):
"Among phenomena" (*dhammesu*) means among the sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*).

"Having thoroughly determined" (*niccheyya*) means having determined, having decided, having investigated, having scrutinized, having weighed, having evaluated, having analyzed, and having made manifest.
“Comprehended” means: grasped by way of a downward grasp, a cavity-grasp, a peak-grasp, a part-grasp, a heap-grasp, or a collection-grasp;
taken as “this is true, real, factual, such as it is, and not otherwise”; clung to, adhered to, obsessed by, and intent upon.
[That] does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtained; it has been abandoned and cut off.
"Stilled, calmed, incapable of arising again, burnt away by the fire of knowledge"—
thus one has discerned and grasped the truth among all phenomena.
Therefore, one transcends all disputes.

Therefore, for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, by that source, he has transcended, surpassed, overcome, and passed beyond disputes of views, quarrels over views, conflicts of views, contentions over views, and strife over views;
thus, "he has transcended disputes.
For he does not perceive any phenomenon as being superior.

Apart from the foundations of mindfulness, apart from the right efforts, apart from the bases of psychic power, apart from the faculties, apart from the powers, apart from the factors of enlightenment, and apart from the noble eightfold path, there is no other teacher, no other proclaimer of Dhamma, no other group, no other view, no other practice,
and no other path that is supreme, best, distinguished, and foremost.
"He does not see, does not behold, does not look at, does not contemplate, and does not examine the supreme, excellent Dhamma"— that is,
he does not see any other Dhamma as the best.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For the brahmin there is nothing to be led by another;
he has grasped what is well-determined among all phenomena.
Therefore, he has transcended disputes.”
"For one does not see the Dhamma as supreme through conceiving.
"I know, I see; it is just so.
Yet some, through their views, declare that purity is attained."
If he has seen something, what does that matter to him?
Having passed beyond that, they declare purity by means of something else, saying:
"I know, I see; it is exactly so."
"I know" means I know either by the knowledge of others' minds or by the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
"I see" means I see either with the fleshly eye or with the divine eye.
"Just so is this" means that this is thus, real, true, factual, as it is, and not otherwise.
I know it, I see it, and it is exactly so.
Some declare purity through views;
some recluses and brahmins declare through views purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation.

“‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—by means of such a view, some recluses and brahmins claim purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release.
‘The world is not eternal...

[and so on] ...neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’—by means of such a view, some recluses and brahmins claim purification, cleansing, complete purification, liberation, release, and total release.”
"Some declare purification through views:
'For what has he seen that he [should know] this?
Here, "he saw" means he saw by way of knowledge of others' minds, or he saw by way of knowledge of recollection of past lives, or he saw with the fleshly eye, or he saw with the divine eye.
"If he saw it, what was done for him by that?"—
what was accomplished for him by that seeing?
There is no full understanding of suffering; there is no abandoning of its origin; there is no development of the path;
there is no realization of the fruit; there is no eradication and abandoning of lust; there is no eradication and abandoning of hatred; there is no eradication and abandoning of delusion;
there is no eradication and abandoning of the defilements; and there is no cutting off of the round of saṃsāra.
If he has seen anything, what does that matter to him?

Having surpassed it, those sectarians claim purity through something else. They have gone beyond, transcended, and passed over the path of purity, the path of purification, the path of complete purity, the path of cleansing, and the path of total cleansing—namely, apart from the foundations of mindfulness.
"Except for the right efforts, except for the bases of psychic power, except for the faculties, except for the powers,

and except for the factors of enlightenment, there is no other way, they say, speak, declare, illuminate, and express, that leads to purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total release."
Thus, having passed beyond even that, they declare purity by means of another.
Or else, the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, and the Paccekabuddhas,
having transcended and completely surpassed the impure path, the unclean path, the unpurified path, the non-bright path, and the non-wholly-bright path of those sectarian teachers—
Having transcended by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path,
they speak of, declare, say, illuminate, and express purity, purification, complete purification, liberation, emancipation, and total emancipation.
Thus, having overstepped even this, they declare purity by means of something else.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I know, I see; it is exactly so.”
Some declare purification through views; for even if one has seen something, what does that have to do with it?
Having disregarded that, they say purification comes by another means.
A person seeing will perceive name-and-form;
having seen it, he will know that this alone is so.
Whether he sees much or little, let him see.
For the wise do not say that purity comes through that.

"A man seeing sees name-and-form": whether seeing by means of the knowledge of others' minds, or seeing by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, or seeing with the fleshly eye, or with the divine eye.
Or, seeing [them] as permanent, as pleasure, or as self, one sees only name-and-form;
one does not see the arising or the passing away of those phenomena, nor their gratification, their danger, or the escape from them—thus it is said:
"The man who sees sees name-and-form."
"Having seen, he will know: 'This indeed is it.

"Having seen" means having seen by means of the knowledge of others' minds, or having seen by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, or having seen with the fleshly eye, or having seen with the divine eye;
having seen only name-and-form, he will know it as permanent and as pleasant.
Thinking, "He will not know the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, or the escape regarding those phenomena," one sees that he will know only these [very things]—
whether he sees much or little.
Whether one perceives name-and-form as much as it may be or as little as it may be, as permanent, as pleasant, or as self—
let one perceive it as much or as little as one wishes;
for the wise do not say that purity comes through that.
"Wholesome" refers to those who are skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in the foundations of mindfulness,
skilled in the right efforts, skilled in the bases of psychic power, skilled in the faculties, skilled in the powers, skilled in the factors of enlightenment,
skilled in the path, skilled in the fruits, and skilled in Nibbāna; these wholesome qualities [are known] either by the knowledge of others' minds or by the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Whether by the fleshly eye or the divine eye, they do not say, speak, declare, illuminate, or express that purity, purification, complete purification,
liberation, emancipation, or total emancipation comes through the vision of name-and-form;
for the wise do not say that purity is attained thereby.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“A man seeing will perceive name-and-form;
having seen them, he will know them as just these.”
"Whether one sees much or little,
the wise do not say that purity comes through that.
For one who speaks with dogmatic insistence is not easily led to purity."
Those who have formed their views and hold them foremost, asserting that there is beauty in what they rely upon,
proclaim purity therein because they have seen it as such.
"One who speaks dogmatically is not easy to instruct.
One who speaks dogmatically says, "The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false," or "The world is non-eternal... [and so on].
“After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish”—thus he is one who speaks with dogmatic adherence.
For he is not one who has well understood.
"One who speaks with dogmatic adherence is difficult to discipline, difficult to instruct, difficult to convince, difficult to lead to right view, and difficult to inspire with confidence;
indeed, one who speaks with dogmatic adherence is not easily disciplined.
They hold fast to views that have been preconceived."
Having fashioned, prepared, contrived, and established [views], one wanders making views the foremost.
One wanders with views as a banner, views as a standard, views as a governing authority, and surrounded by views—thus it is said:
“having fashioned views and placing them foremost.”
"Depending on which, one speaks of beauty therein.

"Depending on which" means: depending on which teacher, teaching of the Dhamma, assembly, view, practice, or path; being dependent, not independent, attached, approached, clung to, and intent upon—that is "depending on which."
"Regarding that": by means of one's own view, one's own inclination, one's own preference, and one's own tenet.

"One who speaks of beauty" means one who speaks of beauty, one who speaks of what is beautiful, one who speaks like a wise man, one who speaks firmly, one who speaks according to the method, one who speaks with reason, one who speaks according to characteristics, one who speaks according to cause, one who speaks according to the proper ground—that is, by means of one's own tenet;
thus, "one who speaks of beauty therein" refers to that upon which one relies.
"Speaking of purity there, having seen it as it is":
this means speaking of purity, speaking of purification, speaking of complete purification, speaking of cleansing, speaking of thorough cleansing;
or alternatively, one who sees purity, sees purification, sees complete purification, sees cleansing, and sees thorough cleansing.
"Purity is his doctrine.

Therein, with his own view, his own inclination, his own preference, and his own conviction, he saw, beheld, perceived, and penetrated that which is real, true, factual, as it is, and unperverted—thus:
"Purity is his doctrine; therein he saw it as it really is."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"One who speaks dogmatically is not easily led;
he is one who has formed views and holds them foremost."
"Whatever basis he relies upon while professing beauty there,
he who professes purity there has seen it as it truly is.
Thus the brahmin does not engage in conceptual construction.
He does not take views as his essence,
nor is he a kinsman of mere knowledge; having understood the various conventional designations,
he remains equanimous, as if regarding them as a mere grasping.
"A Brahmin does not undergo reckoning for an eon.
This is a negation.
One is called a "Brahmin" because of having cast out the seven qualities... [as it is said] "...unattached and such-like, he is called a Brahmā."
“Eras” means two eras:
the era of craving and the era of views … [as before] … this is the era of craving … [as before] …
This is the conceptualization of views.
"Calculation" (saṅkhā) is said to be knowledge.
It is wisdom, understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
"A brahmin does not enter into conceptual proliferation (*saṅkhā*).
A brahmin, having known by means of conceptualization, having weighed, having scrutinized, having analyzed, and having made it manifest, [realizes]:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are impermanent..."
"Having reckoned, known, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that 'all conditioned phenomena are suffering'... and 'whatever has the nature of arising,
all that has the nature of cessation,' one does not lead or adhere to the sphere of craving or the sphere of views."
He does not approach, he does not grasp, he does not cling, and he does not adhere;
thus, the brahmin does not enter into the reckoning of time.
He does not take views as his essence, nor is he bound by knowledge.
His sixty-two types of views have been abandoned, uprooted, calmed, and stilled; they are incapable of arising again and have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge.

He does not go along with views, is not led by them, is not carried away by them, is not swept off by them, nor does he regard those views as essential or return to them; thus, he is "one who does not take views as his essence."

"Nor is he one who has knowledge as his bond": by means of the knowledge of the eight attainments or the knowledge of the five higher powers, he does not create, generate, produce, bring about, or cause to arise a bond of craving or a bond of views;
thus, "he does not take views as his essence, nor has knowledge as his bond.
And having known the various conventional designations of worldlings...
“Having known” means having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest. Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified,
and made manifest that “all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” [and] having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified,
and made manifest that “all conditioned phenomena are suffering,” and so forth...
“Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and clarified that ‘whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation’—having made it manifest, thus ‘having known,’ he [says this].
Conventional designations (sammuti) are said to be the sixty-two types of views; these are the conventional designations of views.”
They are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*) because they are produced by worldlings, or because they are conventional designations (*sammuti*) produced by them;
alternatively, they are "worldlings" because they are conventional designations produced by various diverse people (*puthu-nānājana*).
Having understood these worldly conventions,
he remains equanimous, yet he conceives of this as "grasping. Others, however,
through the influence of craving and views, grasp, misapprehend, and adhere to them.
“The Arahant observes with equanimity; he does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere”—thus, “he observes” implies “he grasps.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The Brahmin does not enter into conceptual construction,
nor does he rely on views, nor is he a kinsman of mere knowledge;
having understood the various conventional designations, [he transcends them].”
"I think he maintains equanimity even toward grasping.
Having cast aside all bonds in this world,
the Sage does not side with any faction amidst the arising of disputes.
He is equanimous toward the good and the bad;
I consider him one who, though ungrasping, is truly grasping.
Having cast off all bonds, the sage surveys this world.
"Knots" refers to the four knots:
the bodily knot of covetousness, the bodily knot of ill will, the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily knot of insistence on "this alone is the truth.
Covetousness for one's own view is the bodily knot of covetousness; resentment and hostility toward the doctrines of others is the bodily knot of ill will.
The bodily tie of clinging to rules and observances is the misapprehension of one's own virtue, vow, or combination of virtue and vow;
the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence is the insistence that "only this is the truth.
Having relinquished means having abandoned the ties. Having released means having let go of them.
Or else, having loosened the knots— whether they be knotted, tightly knotted, bound, firmly bound, fastened, stuck, firmly stuck, obstructed, or fettered— and having released them:
just as they prepare, release, and dismantle a draft animal, a chariot, a cart, or a carriage when it is hitched up,
even so, having cast off the knots, one releases them.
Alternatively, having loosened and released the knots—those that are knotted, entwined, bound, obstructed, fastened, stuck, clung to, impeded, the bond itself—the Sage (muni).
"Sage" (muni): wisdom (ñāṇa) is called *mona* ... [as before] ... having transcended the net of attachment, he is a sage.
"Here" means in this view...
[and so on] ...in this human world—
the sage here in the world has laid aside all ties.
"Among those who have arisen into disputes":
when disputes have arisen, been produced, been brought forth, and become manifest;

when they are proceeding through favoritism (*chandāgati*), proceeding through ill-will (*dosāgati*), proceeding through fear (*bhayāgati*), or proceeding through delusion (*mohāgati*)—one does not follow favoritism.
He goes; he does not go by way of hatred, he does not go by way of fear, he does not go by way of delusion;
he does not go under the influence of lust, he does not go under the influence of hatred, he does not go under the influence of delusion;
he does not go under the influence of conceit, he does not go under the influence of views, he does not go under the influence of restlessness, nor under the influence of doubt.

He goes, but he does not go by way of underlying tendencies; he is not led, carried away, swept off, or dragged along by partisan doctrines—thus, amidst those born of dispute, he does not follow the faction.
He is one who is peaceful and equanimous toward the unpeaceful.
They are "peaceful" because they have calmed passion; they are peaceful because they have calmed hatred; they are peaceful because they have calmed delusion...

[and so on] ...because they have calmed, stilled, pacified, extinguished, quenched, removed, and tranquillized all unwholesome volitional formations, they are called "peaceful, calmed, pacified, quenched, and tranquillized."

The peaceful among the unpeaceful: "Among the unpeaceful" means among those who have not attained peace, who have not become tranquil, who have not attained Nibbāna, and who have not reached full composure;
thus, "the peaceful among the unpeaceful."
"Equanimous is that Arahant, endowed with the sixfold equanimity; having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on for the other senses] ...he awaits his time, developed and self-controlled."
He is equanimous toward those who are not virtuous.
He thinks, "I am one who assists," while others,
through craving and through views, grasp, misapprehend, and adhere [to them].
“The Arahant observes with equanimity; he does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere”—this seems to be an assistance, yet it is called grasping.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having cast off all bonds in this world,
the Sage does not side with those caught in disputes;
being peaceful among the unpeaceful, he remains equanimous.”
"I think that grasping is a favor.
Having abandoned past defilements and not creating new ones,
one who is not led by desire and does not dogmatically adhere to views—
The wise one, liberated from views,
is not stained by the world, nor does he reproach himself.
Having abandoned past defilements, he commits no new ones.
"Former taints" refers to past form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
Having abandoned, relinquished, completely renounced, discarded, dispelled, brought to an end, and caused to cease those defilements that might arise with reference to past formations—
this is "having abandoned former taints."
They do not create new [karmic formations]; thus they are called "new.

These are the presently arisen form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Not creating desire, not creating affection, not creating lust, not generating, not producing, not bringing forth, and not giving rise to volitional formations with respect to the present—thus, "having abandoned the old, he does not create the new."
"One who is not led by desire nor one who speaks out of attachment.
This means he does not go astray through desire, he does not go astray through hatred, he does not go astray through delusion, he does not go astray through fear;
he does not act under the influence of lust, he does not act under the influence of hatred, and he does not act under the influence of delusion.
He does not proceed by way of conceit, he does not proceed by way of views, he does not proceed by way of restlessness,
he does not proceed by way of doubt, he does not proceed by way of underlying tendencies;
he is not carried away, led, swept along, or dragged about by factional doctrines.
He is not one who follows desire. Nor is he one who speaks dogmatically; that is, he does not speak dogmatically, saying, "The world is eternal;

this alone is true, all else is false," nor does he speak dogmatically, saying, "After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is true, all else is false. ... [and so on] ... nor does he speak dogmatically, saying, "After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
He is neither led by desire nor is he one who dogmatically adheres to views.

That wise man is completely liberated from the sixty-two types of views; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; they are rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge.
Being thus liberated from the grip of views, he dwells with a mind that is detached and free from the boundaries of conceptualization.
“Wise” means wise, learned, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowing, discerning, and sagacious—
he is the wise one who is liberated from views.
“He is not smeared in the world, nor does he reproach himself.”
There are two kinds of clinging:
the clinging of craving and the clinging of views... [as above] ...this is the clinging of craving... [as above] ...
This is the smear of views.
For him, the smear of craving has been abandoned and the smear of views has been relinquished;
because the smear of craving has been abandoned and the smear of views has been relinquished, he is not smeared by the world of the lower realms.
He is not smeared in the world of humans; he is not smeared in the world of devas; he is not smeared in the world of the aggregates;
he is not smeared in the world of the elements; he is not smeared, nor defiled, nor stained in the world of the sense bases.
Unsmearable, undefiled, unstained, he dwells emerged, escaped, liberated, detached, with a mind for which the boundaries of the conditioned have been transcended.
He is not stained in the world.
"One who reproaches oneself" reproaches oneself for two reasons: on account of what has been done and on account of what has not been done.
How does one reproach oneself on account of what has been done and what has not been done?
One reproaches oneself, thinking: "I have committed bodily misconduct; I have failed to perform bodily good conduct. [One reproaches oneself, thinking:
"I have committed verbal misconduct... and so forth.
He reproaches himself, thinking: "I have committed misconduct of mind...
I have committed the taking of life...
[and so on]... I have held wrong view; I have not cultivated right view."
Thus he reproaches himself for what has been done and what has not been done. Or else, he reproaches himself, thinking,
"I have not fulfilled my duties regarding the moral precepts," or "I have not guarded the doors of the sense faculties."
“I am immoderate in eating,” … “I am not devoted to wakefulness,” … “I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. …
“I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness” … “I have not developed the four right efforts” … “I have not developed the four bases for psychic power” …
“Five faculties have not been developed by me,” … “five powers have not been developed by me,” … “seven factors of enlightenment have not been developed by me.”
‘The noble eightfold path has not been developed by me’ … ‘Suffering has not been fully understood by me’ … ‘The origin of suffering has not been abandoned by me’ …
“‘The path has not been cultivated by me’ … ‘Cessation has not been realized by me,’ he blames himself.
Thus he blames himself for what has been done and for what has not been done.”
Thus one is self-reproaching.
But by not performing that action, not producing it, not generating it, not bringing it about, not causing its manifestation, one is not self-reproaching;
thus, being not self-reproaching, one is not smeared in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having abandoned past defilements and not creating new ones,
one who is free from favoritism and does not dogmatically adhere to views;”
That wise one, liberated from views,
is not stained by the world, being free from self and reproach.
He has become disengaged from all phenomena.
Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed,
the sage who has laid down the burden is fully liberated;
he does not speculate, he does not strive for restraint, nor does he long for anything.
(Thus said the Blessed One:
He has become free from the army among all phenomena—whatever is seen, heard, or sensed.
"Army" refers to the army of Māra.
Bodily misconduct is Māra’s army; verbal misconduct is Māra’s army; mental misconduct is Māra’s army. Greed... hatred...
delusion... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... envy... avarice... deceit... craftiness... obstinacy...
aggression... conceit... arrogance... vanity... negligence... all defilements... all forms of misconduct [are Māra’s army].
...all distresses ... all fevers ... all torments ... all unwholesome volitional formations are Māra’s army.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Sensual pleasures are your first army..."
The second is called discontentment...
A coward does not conquer it.
“Having conquered, one obtains happiness. Since,
by means of the four noble paths, the entire army of Māra, all adversaries, and all defilements have been conquered, defeated, shattered, broken apart, and turned away—
he is called one who has become free from the enemy host.
Thus, being detached from what is seen, from what is heard, from what is sensed, and from what is cognized...
"Regarding what is cognized,
he has become free from the army"— he is free from the army among all phenomena, whatever is seen, heard, or sensed. "That sage,
having laid down the burden, is utterly released."
There are three burdens:
the burden of the aggregates, the burden of the defilements, and the burden of volitional formations.
What is the burden of the aggregates?
At rebirth-linking, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
this is the burden of the aggregates.
What is the burden of defilements?
Greed, hatred, and delusion …pe… all unwholesome volitional formations—
this is the burden of defilement.
What is the burden of volitional formations?
The formation of merit, the formation of demerit, and the formation of the imperturbable—
this is the burden of volitional formations.
When the burden of the aggregates, the burden of the defilements, and the burden of volitional formations have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future, he is said to be one who has laid down the burden, dropped the burden, relinquished the burden,
fully set down the burden, cast off the burden, and whose burden has become tranquil.
"Moni": "Mona" is said to be knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

It is that which is wisdom (*paññā*), understanding (*pajānanā*), investigation (*vicaya*), thorough investigation (*pavicaya*), investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), discernment (*sallakkhaṇā*), close discernment (*upalakkhaṇā*), precise discernment (*paccupalakkhaṇā*), sagacity (*paṇḍiccaṃ*), skillfulness (*kosallaṃ*), subtlety (*nepuññaṃ*), discrimination (*vebhabyā*), reflection (*cintā*), examination (*upaparikkhā*), vastness (*bhūri*), intelligence (*medhā*), guidance (*parināyikā*), and insight (*vipassanā*).

Clear comprehension is a goad; it is wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, and right view.
Endowed with that knowledge, the sage has attained sagehood.
There are three types of nobility:
nobility of body, nobility of speech, and nobility of mind.
What is nobility of body?
The abandoning of the three kinds of bodily misconduct is bodily integrity; the three kinds of bodily good conduct are bodily integrity;
knowledge regarding the body as an object is bodily integrity; full understanding of the body is bodily integrity; the path accompanied by full understanding is bodily integrity;
the abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily integrity; the cessation of bodily formations through the attainment of the fourth jhāna is bodily integrity.
This is bodily integrity.
What is verbal integrity?
The abandoning of the four kinds of verbal misconduct is verbal integrity; the four kinds of verbal good conduct are verbal integrity.
Knowledge regarding the object of speech is verbal refinement; full understanding of speech is verbal refinement; the path accompanied by full understanding is verbal refinement;

the abandoning of desire and lust for speech is verbal refinement; the cessation of the mental formations of speech, which is the attainment of the second jhāna, is verbal refinement—this is verbal refinement.
What is purity of mind?
The abandoning of the three kinds of mental misconduct is purity of mind; the three kinds of mental good conduct are purity of mind;
knowledge regarding the object of consciousness is purity of mind; full understanding of consciousness is purity of mind; and the path accompanied by full understanding is purity of mind.

Mental silence is the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind; mental silence is the cessation of mental formations; mental silence is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling—this is mental silence.
“Silent in body, silent in speech, ...”
The sage whose mind is silent and free from taints, who is perfected in sagacity,
they call the one who has abandoned everything.
The Sage of body, the Sage of speech,
the Sage of mind, free from taints;
the Sage endowed with sagacity—
“They have washed away their evil,” they say.
Possessed of these three qualities of sagacity, there are six types of sages:
the householder sage, the homeless sage, the trainee sage, the one beyond training sage, the paccekabuddha sage, and the sage of sages.
Who are the household sages?
Those householders who have seen the state and understood the teaching—
these are the household sages.
Who are the homeless sages?
Those who have gone forth, who have seen the state and understood the teaching—
these are the homeless sages.
The seven trainees are the sages-in-training; the arahants are the sages beyond training.
The paccekabuddhas are the solitary sages.
The Tathāgatas, the arahants, the perfectly enlightened ones, are called the sages of sages.
“One does not become a sage by silence,
being dull-witted and ignorant; but he who,
like one holding a scale, [discerns the truth]...”
Having taken up the superior choice, the wise man avoids all evils;
because of that, he is a sage, a true muni.
He who understands both worlds is therefore called a sage (muni).
Having known the Dhamma of both the non-existent and the existent, he is called a sage.
Within and without, throughout the entire world—
he who is honored by gods and humans,
having utterly transcended the net of attachments, he is the Sage.
"Completely liberated": the mind of the Sage is released from lust, liberated, well-liberated;
the mind is released from hatred … from delusion, liberated, well-liberated …pe…
"His mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from all unwholesome volitional formations"—
thus he is the sage who has laid down the burden, who is utterly freed.
"He is not a theorist, he is stilled, he is not one who yearns"— such is the Blessed One.
Eras are of two kinds:
the era of craving and the era of views...
[as above] ...this is the era of craving... [as above] ...
This is the conceptualization of views.
For him, the conceptualization of craving has been abandoned and the conceptualization of views has been relinquished.

Because the conceptualization of craving has been abandoned and the conceptualization of views has been relinquished, he does not conceptualize, generate, produce, bring about, or cause to arise either the conceptualization of craving or the conceptualization of views.
It is not allowable.
"Not dispassionate" means:
all foolish worldlings are impassioned; starting from the virtuous worldling, the seven trainees are impassioned regarding what has not yet been attained.
They delight in, abstain from, and refrain from [unwholesome states] for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, for the sake of realizing what has not been realized;
the Arahant is removed, abstained, and refrained; he has gone forth, emerged, and is fully liberated;
he dwells with a mind that is detached and free from boundaries—thus it is said.
It is not allowable;
it is not ceased.
"Not desired" means that "desire" (patthanā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ...

covetousness, greed, and root of unwholesomeness there is—when this aspiration and craving have been abandoned by one, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge, he is called "one who does not aspire.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence.
Moreover, he is called the Blessed One because he has destroyed lust;
he is called the Blessed One because he has destroyed hatred; he is called the Blessed One because he has destroyed delusion.
The Blessed One has destroyed conceit;
the Blessed One has destroyed wrong views;
the Blessed One has destroyed the thorns [of defilement].
The Blessed One is called "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed the defilements;
he is called "Bhagavā" because he has possessed, analyzed, and fully analyzed the jewel of the Dhamma;
he is called "Bhagavā" because he has brought an end to the states of existence.
The Blessed One has cultivated the body, cultivated virtue, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom;
or, the Blessed One frequented remote forest and woodland dwellings—places of little noise, little sound, secluded from people, hidden away from men, and suitable for retreat;
or, the Blessed One was a partaker of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; thus he is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma, and the flavor of liberation; he possesses higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom.
Or, the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
Or, the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive dwellings in attainment.

The Blessed One is a partaker of the ten developments of perception, the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the attainment of the foul; thus he is the Blessed One.

Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; thus he is the Blessed One.

The Blessed One is a possessor of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the six qualities of a Buddha—thus he is called "Bhagavā.

This name "Bhagavā" was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by friends and colleagues, nor by kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities.
This is the definitive designation of the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree, co-arising with the attainment of omniscient knowledge: namely, "the Blessed One" (Bhagavā).
He is not one who fancies himself, nor is he one who has ceased, nor is he one who desires; thus is he the Blessed One.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He who has become free from hostility toward all phenomena—
whatever is seen, heard, or sensed—
is a sage with his burden laid down, utterly liberated.”
“Neither permissible, nor restrained, nor aspiring.
(Thus said the Blessed One.
The thirteenth exposition, the Mahābyūha Sutta.
